question: While she's on call, how fast does Ortega have to answer a page and get to the hospital? Is she otherwise restricted?
source: On-Call Compensation Policy HR-214 (rev. 3, effective January 1, 2024)
evidence: While on call, an employee must answer a page within ten (10) minutes and must be able to report to the facility within forty-five (45) minutes of being called back. … Subject to those two requirements, the employee is otherwise free to use on-call time for his or her own purposes

also.source: Demand letter from Reyes & Gold for Maria Ortega (October 6, 2026)
also.evidence: Under HR-214, Ms. Ortega must answer every page within ten minutes and must be able to report to Lakeshore Medical Center within forty-five minutes.

note: Section 3.3: answer a page within 10 minutes and be able to report within 45 minutes; otherwise free to use the time for her own purposes (sleep at home, family, errands within range), with no requirement to stay on the premises, wear a uniform or work unless called back. The demand letter argues these limits make the time 'engaged to wait'; the HR memo (6.2) says therapists are free to stay home, sleep and handle personal matters.

question: How long does the tolling agreement run, and can either side end it early?
source: Tolling agreement - Maria Ortega and Ridgeline (signed October 28, 2026)
evidence: "Tolling Period" means the period from October 6, 2026 through January 31, 2027, inclusive, unless it is ended earlier under section 3.2. | Either Party may end the Tolling Period earlier by giving the other Party fifteen (15) days' written notice.
note: The Tolling Period runs from October 6, 2026 (the demand letter's date) through January 31, 2027, ending at 11:59 p.m. Central Time unless extended in writing. Either party may end it earlier on fifteen (15) days' written notice, sent by email and overnight courier (3.3). Signed October 28, 2026; no admission of liability (4.1); Illinois law (6.1).

question: At the policy rates, what would 214 weeknights and 31 weekend days of on-call come to? Does the demand letter's stipend figure hold up?

evidence: Ms. Ortega is owed $41,200.00 in on-call stipends calculated at Ridgeline's own policy rates for the 214 weeknights and 31 weekend days on which she was on call during the period.

also.source: On-Call Compensation Policy HR-214 (rev. 3, effective January 1, 2024)
also.evidence: receives a stipend of $95.00 per weeknight | receives a stipend of $240.00 per weekend or holiday day

note: 214 x $95.00 = $20,330.00 and 31 x $240.00 = $7,440.00, total $27,770.00, not the $41,200.00 claimed ($13,430.00 too high). Of the $27,770.00, Ridgeline actually paid $26,250.00 (payroll register), leaving the 16 unpaid weeknights ($1,520.00).

question: Is the $57.00 overtime rate in the demand letter consistent with Ortega's pay terms?
evidence: You will be paid $38.00 per hour | This means that you are eligible for overtime at one and one-half times (1.5x) your regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek.

also.source: Demand letter from Reyes & Gold for Maria Ortega (October 6, 2026)
also.evidence: each should have been paid at one and one-half times her regular rate, or $57.00 per hour

note: Yes: 1.5 x $38.00 = $57.00, so the overtime rate (and 126 x $57.00 = $7,182.00) is arithmetically right. But the payroll register shows 88 of the 126 hours were already paid at $57.00 and the other 38 fell in weeks under 40 hours.

question: The demand letter treats all 126 call-back hours as unpaid overtime worth $7,182. What does payroll show?
source: Payroll register extract - Maria Ortega, on-call stipends and call-back pay
evidence: Total | 88.00 | 5,016.00 | 38.00 | 1,444.00 | 126.00 | 6,460.00 | The 38.00 CB-REG hours were worked in workweeks in which Ms. Ortega's total hours worked, including the call-back time, were under 40, and were therefore paid at the regular rate under Policy HR-214, section 4.1.

also.source: Demand letter from Reyes & Gold for Maria Ortega (October 6, 2026)
also.evidence: Her unpaid overtime is therefore 126 call-back hours at $57.00 per hour, or $7,182.00.
Payroll confirmed that the 38 hours paid at the regular rate fell in weeks under 40 hours, counting the call-back time.

note: All 126 hours were paid: 88 at $57.00 (1.5x) = $5,016.00 for hours over 40, and 38 at the regular $38.00 = $1,444.00 because they fell in weeks under 40 hours (total $6,460.00). The $7,182.00 is arithmetically right (126 x $57.00) but ignores what was paid, and on the current hours no overtime premium was due on the 38 hours; it would turn on the demand's theory that on-call time is hours worked.

question: What does HR recommend we do about the on-call pay problem?

note: Three recommendations (Janet Kowalski, October 20, 2026): (1) pay Ms. Ortega $1,520.00 plus interest, coordinated with outside counsel because she is represented; (2) pay the eleven other affected employees their unpaid amounts plus interest once Payroll's schedule is final; (3) audit all Kronos schedule templates at every facility against HR-214 section 5.1 and make sure the section 6.5 post-upgrade testing is done.
